gloss_terse: To lift, carry, bear; by extension: to take, forgive, endure, exalt; physical raising, transport, moral bearing
gloss_readable: One of the most versatile verbs in the Hebrew Bible, nasa spans a remarkable range from concrete to abstract. At its physical core it means to lift up (eyes, hands, voice) or to carry a burden. Yet the same root bears the weight of forgiveness when God 'lifts away' sin, and of endurance when a person 'bears' guilt. It appears in charged idioms: nasa panim ('lift the face') signals partiality, while nasa rosh ('lift the head') can mean to honor or to take a census. The Piel intensifies to 'sustain,' the Hitpael captures reflexive self-exaltation. Spanish distinguishes alzar (lift) from llevar (carry) and perdonar (forgive), confirming the real semantic splits.

senses.1: The foundational Qal sense of physically lifting or raising something upward — eyes toward the horizon (Gen 18:2), hands in prayer, or a voice in lamentation. Spanish alzar and French lever consistently distinguish this from carrying. At 330 occurrences it is the verb's gravitational center, always implying upward motion or elevation.
senses.2: Carrying a physical load or transporting persons and objects, as in bearing the ark on poles (Exod 25:14) or wagons carrying Jacob's family to Egypt (Gen 46:5). German tragen and Spanish llevar mark this as sustained horizontal movement rather than the upward lift of Sense 1. Participle forms yield agent nouns: 'armor-bearer,' 'burden-bearer.'
senses.3: Taking, receiving, or obtaining — a wife, a gift, a census. The idiom nasa rosh ('lift the head' = 'take a count') appears prominently in Numbers (Num 1:2). Spanish Tomen and French pris signal acquisition rather than physical motion. Also covers accepting or receiving favor (Gen 27:3, Exod 20:7).
senses.4: The profound theological sense of forgiving or removing sin, as when Abraham intercedes for Sodom (Gen 18:24–26) or Joseph's brothers plead nasa pesha (Gen 50:17). Spanish perdonar and German vergeben confirm a distinct forgiveness meaning. The Qal passive participle ashre nesu pesha ('blessed is the one whose transgression is lifted away,' Ps 32:1) crystallizes this sense.
senses.5: The Niphal (passive/reflexive) of being lifted up or exalted — hills that 'are raised' (Isa 2:2), a kingdom 'exalted' (1 Chr 14:2). Spanish elevada and enaltecido consistently mark passive exaltation. Distinguished from the active Qal by grammatical stem and by describing a state rather than an action.
senses.6: Bearing or enduring guilt, blame, or punishment as consequence — not forgiveness (Sense 4) but suffering. When the land 'cannot bear' both Abram and Lot (Gen 13:6), or Moses protests he cannot 'bear' the people alone (Deut 1:12), the subject absorbs the weight rather than removing it. Spanish cargado con ('burdened with') and French porter confirm the endurance nuance.
senses.7: The idiom nasa panim ('lift the face'), meaning to show partiality or favoritism. Deuteronomy 10:17 declares God does not 'lift faces,' meaning He shows no favoritism. Spanish acepcion de personas and German Ansehen der Person capture the social-bias meaning that distinguishes this from mere physical lifting of Sense 1.
senses.8: The Piel intensive stem used for actively exalting, sustaining, or supporting someone — God exalted David's kingdom (2 Sam 5:12), or Cyrus's decree that neighbors should 'supply' returning exiles (Ezra 1:4). The factitive force means 'cause to be lifted,' stronger and more deliberate than simple Qal lifting.
senses.9: The Hitpael reflexive-intensive: to exalt oneself or be exalted reflexively. Korah's rebellion opens with the accusation 'why do you exalt yourselves?' (Num 16:3). Spanish enalteceis and French exalter vous-memes confirm the self-directed meaning. Only three occurrences, but theologically pointed.
senses.10: Carrying away by force — wind sweeping away like chaff (Isa 64:6), a lion snatching a lamb (1 Sam 17:34), or watchmen stripping away a garment (Song 5:7). Spanish arrastrar ('drag away') and German abtragen ('carry off') mark violent removal distinct from voluntary transport.
senses.11: Wearing garments or bearing equipment upon one's person: the priest Ahijah 'wearing' the ephod (1 Sam 14:3), or the eighty-five priests 'wearing' linen ephods (1 Sam 22:18). Spanish vestir and portador de confirm adornment or personal equipment rather than transport.
senses.12: A narrow usage in 2 Sam 8:2 and 8:6 where the conquered Moabites and Arameans 'became bearers of tribute.' All languages use 'bearers of' (portadores de, bearers de/von), marking a specialized political-economic sense of tributary burden-bearing.
senses.13: The Qal passive participle used for those who are honored or esteemed — 'those lifted up' (Isa 46:3, referring to Israel carried from the womb). Spanish llevados ('the carried ones') and the context of divine maternal care distinguish this from military or census passive senses.
senses.14: The rare Hifil causative: to cause others to bear. In Lev 22:16 priests 'cause them to bear the iniquity of guilt,' and in 2 Sam 17:13 ropes would 'bring' a city to the valley. German cause-them-to-bear and Spanish haran llevar confirm the causative structure.
senses.15: A singular occurrence at Exod 23:1 — 'you shall not lift up a false report.' Spanish levantaras and French elever en haut maintain the basic 'raise' semantics, but the legal context (bearing false witness) gives it a juridical edge not found in the generic Sense 1.
senses.16: At Ps 16:4 — 'I will not take up their names upon my lips.' Spanish tomare and German erhob suggest 'take up' in the sense of adopting or uttering, a refusal to invoke pagan deity names.
senses.17: At Gen 19:21 — 'I have lifted your face' (granted your request), a divine concession to Lot. Spanish he levantado and French j'ai eleve show acceptance/favor, combining the 'lift face' idiom with a divine-response context unique among nasa occurrences.
senses.18: At Isa 18:3 — 'when a signal is lifted on the mountains.' Spanish cuando alzar and French lever point to the raising of a military standard or signal, a public-display nuance connected to warfare signaling.
senses.19: At Ps 28:2 — 'when I lift up my hands toward your holy sanctuary.' Spanish cuando alzo and French porter confirm prayer gesture. While related to Sense 1 (lifting), the liturgical specificity of hands-toward-the-sanctuary sets it apart.
senses.20: At 1 Kgs 2:26 — 'you carried the ark of the Lord God.' Spanish llevaste and French tu emporta confirm bearing/carrying, but this single address to Abiathar functions as a credential-recitation, acknowledging past faithful service as grounds for mercy.

gloss_terse: To be or grow strong, seize, repair, harden; covers courage, physical grasping, building restoration, and obstinacy
gloss_readable: A verb of firmness in all its dimensions — physical, moral, and structural. In its Qal intransitive form, hazaq is the great exhortation of the Hebrew Bible: 'be strong and courageous!' (Deut 31:6). Yet the same root, shifted to the Hifil, becomes the hand that seizes Lot's wrist to drag him from Sodom (Gen 19:16) or the craftsman's grip that repairs Jerusalem's walls (Nehemiah passim). The Piel hardens Pharaoh's heart (Exod 4:21) and fastens nails for idols (Jer 10:4). Arabic confirms the splits: tashaddada for inner courage, amsaka for physical grasping, rammama for building repair, and qassa for heart-hardening — four distinct roots mapping onto one Hebrew verb.

senses.1: The intransitive Qal core: to be strong or courageous, the exhortation hazaq ve'emats that echoes through Deuteronomy and Joshua (Deut 31:6–7, Josh 1:6–9). Arabic tashaddada/taqawwa (reflexive strengthening) and Korean 강하다 consistently render inner resolve. At 62 occurrences, this is the motivational heart of the verb.
senses.2: The Hifil sense of physically seizing or grasping — taking hold of a person or object with the hand. Arabic amsaka ('to seize, grasp') uses an entirely different root (m-s-k) from the courage sense, confirming a real semantic break. Lot seized by angels (Gen 19:16), Moses grasping the serpent (Exod 4:4), a man seizing a woman (Deut 22:25).
senses.3: A specialized Hifil participial usage meaning 'repairers of' buildings and walls, concentrated in Nehemiah 3 where it appears as a near-technical term for construction repair. Arabic murammimi ('repairers') uses the root r-m-m, wholly distinct from both 'seize' and 'strengthen,' confirming lexical specialization.
senses.4: The Piel factitive: to strengthen, encourage, or support someone transitively. Deuteronomy's charge to 'encourage Joshua' (Deut 1:38, 3:28) and Judges' pattern of God strengthening enemies as judgment (Judg 3:12). Arabic qawwa (Form II causative, 'to strengthen') and shajja'a ('to encourage') mark the transitive causation.
senses.5: The Hitpael reflexive: to strengthen oneself, muster courage, or rally one's own resolve. David 'strengthened himself in the LORD' after Ziklag (1 Sam 30:6). Arabic tashaddada (Form V reflexive) and Korean 스스로 강하게 하다 confirm the self-directed nature. Twenty-eight occurrences across narrative, prophetic, and wisdom texts.
senses.6: Hifil sense of holding fast or clinging to something in sustained manner — metaphorical loyalty (holding to God, 2 Kgs 18:6), obstinate attachment (holding to deceit, Jer 8:5), or physical retention (1 Kgs 9:9). Arabic tamassaka (Form V, 'to cling to, adhere') maps precisely, confirming an ongoing-state meaning distinct from the momentary 'seize' of Sense 2.
senses.7: The Piel used specifically for repairing or restoring physical structures — the Temple (2 Kgs 12:5–12) and city fortifications. Arabic rammama ('to repair, renovate') is the same distinct root used in the Hifil Nehemiah repairs (Sense 3), showing that both stems converge on building restoration as a specialized domain.
senses.8: The Piel sense of hardening, applied specifically to Pharaoh's heart in Exodus (Exod 4:21, 9:12, 10:20, 10:27, 11:10) and to faces set in obstinacy. Arabic qassa ('to make hard/callous') from root q-s-w is categorically different from qawwa ('to strengthen'), confirming that hardening is a distinct semantic event, not merely intensified strength.
senses.9: The Qal sense of prevailing or overpowering an adversary — competitive superiority in conflict. David prevailed over Goliath (1 Sam 17:50), Amnon overpowered Tamar (2 Sam 13:14). Arabic ghalaba ('to overcome, defeat') supplies yet another distinct root, separating martial victory from mere inherent strength (Sense 1).
senses.10: The Qal used for the intensification or severity of impersonal conditions — famine growing severe (Gen 41:56), battle intensifying, Pharaoh's heart 'being strong' against the plagues (Exod 7:13). Arabic ishtadda (Form VIII, 'to become intense/severe') marks escalation of a situation rather than personal strength or courage.
senses.11: The Piel sense of fastening or securing physical objects — nailing down idols so they won't topple (Jer 10:4, Isa 41:7), making ropes hold firm (Isa 33:23). Arabic thabbata ('to fix in place') from root th-b-t confirms a distinct 'secure/fasten' meaning separate from both 'repair' and 'strengthen.'
senses.12: A rare Hifil sense of prevailing or being victorious with resultative force beyond the Qal 'prevail.' In Job 18:9 a trap 'prevails' over the wicked, and Dan 11:32 promises those who know God 'shall be strong' in ultimate triumph. Arabic yazfaru ('to triumph') marks the culminative victory.
senses.13: At Exod 12:33 — the Egyptians 'urged' the Israelites to leave in haste after the final plague. English 'urged,' Spanish apremiaba ('pressed'), and the context of desperate pressure after death show an interpersonal 'press/urge' sense distinct from mere physical strengthening.
senses.14: At Isa 39:1 — Hezekiah 'had recovered' from his illness. Spanish se habia fortalecido ('had strengthened himself') and the narrative of convalescence show a medical-recovery sense: regaining physical health after sickness.
senses.15: At 2 Chr 28:20 — Tilgath-pilneser 'did not strengthen' Ahaz but rather distressed him. The ironic negation (came to help but actually weakened) makes this a failed-support instance. Spanish lo fortalecio confirms the expected 'strengthen' meaning, but the narrative subverts it.
senses.16: At 2 Kgs 4:8 — the Shunammite woman 'urged' Elisha to eat. Spanish lo insistio ('insisted to him') and the hospitality context show social pressure or earnest persuasion, parallel to the Egyptian urgency of Sense 13 but in a gracious rather than desperate setting.
senses.17: At Lev 25:35 — 'you shall strengthen him' (support a fellow Israelite who becomes poor). Spanish lo sostendras ('you shall sustain him') frames economic mutual aid. This is transitive Piel encouragement (like Sense 4) but specialized to financial support of the vulnerable.
senses.18: At 2 Sam 18:9 — Absalom's head 'caught' in the oak branches. Spanish se atoro ('got stuck') and English 'caught' show an involuntary entanglement, where the tree's grip is the agent. A passive-accidental 'seize' distinct from the deliberate grasping of Sense 2.

gloss_terse: To strike, smite, beat, kill; covers warfare, physical blows, divine affliction, defeat, and wounding
gloss_readable: Almost exclusively a Hifil verb, nakah is the Bible's primary word for violent striking — from battlefield slaughter to a parent's discipline to God's plagues upon Egypt. Its range moves from the concrete (a hand striking a cheek) to the cosmic (the LORD striking a nation with pestilence). Multilingual evidence sharply distinguishes its subsenses: Arabic uses daraba for generic striking but jaraha for wounding, qatala for killing, and safaqa for clapping; Spanish separates herir (wound) from matar (kill) and golpear (beat). The rare Hofal and Niphal passives appear when the struck party is foregrounded, while a few occurrences extend the root metaphorically to hail destroying crops or hands clapping in ceremony.

senses.1: The dominant military Hifil: to strike or smite enemies in battle, accounting for 362 of 502 occurrences. From Moses striking the Egyptian (Exod 2:12) to the conquest narratives of Joshua, this is the standard term for martial violence. All languages use their generic 'strike' verb — Spanish hirio, French frappa, German schlug — confirming a broad, undifferentiated combat sense.
senses.2: Non-lethal physical striking: beating, hitting, or disciplining a person outside of warfare. Korean ttaerida ('beat, hit personally') replaces the generic chida used for battle, and Spanish azoto ('whipped') signals corporal punishment. Exod 2:11 (Egyptian beating a Hebrew) and the legal casuistry of Exod 21 exemplify this interpersonal-violence sense.
senses.3: Striking with lethal result — to kill or slay. Distinguished by Spanish mataron/matador ('they killed/killer'), Arabic yaqtul ('to kill'), and Swahili kuwaua ('to cause death'). The avenger-of-blood passages (Josh 20:3, 9) and Gen 4:15 (Cain's protection) show this as purposeful, death-dealing violence.
senses.4: Divine affliction: God striking with plague, disease, blindness, or curse. Deut 28:22–35 catalogs afflictions — consumption, fever, boils, madness — each introduced by nakah. Arabic daraba plus prepositional phrases and first-person divine speech ('I struck you') set this apart from human combat.
senses.5: To defeat or overcome, a figurative extension where the emphasis falls on the outcome (victory/conquest) rather than the physical blow. Spanish vencer/derrotar ('conquer/defeat') and Swahili kushinda ('to win') appear here instead of the generic 'strike' glosses. Gen 14:17 (Abraham's defeat of the kings) and Deut 29:7 typify this sense.
senses.6: The Hofal passive: to be struck or smitten. Used of persons beaten in battle (Exod 5:14), cities conquered, or individuals afflicted. Sixteen occurrences including participles describing a state of having-been-struck. French battu and Spanish golpeada/herido confirm passive voice.
senses.7: Hifil striking directed at a non-personal entity — land, city, water, rock, or ground. Feminine pronominal suffixes and neuter 'it' in English mark the inanimate object. Num 14:12 (striking the land with pestilence), Josh 10:28–30 (striking cities), and Num 22:25 (the donkey struck against a wall) illustrate this pattern.
senses.8: Wounding or injuring without death — a specialized subset where Arabic jaraha ('to wound') replaces the usual daraba. The assassination attempts on kings (2 Kgs 8:29, 9:15) and the murder of Sennacherib (2 Kgs 19:37) where the focus is on injury rather than immediate death mark this sense.
senses.9: Clapping hands — a metaphorical extension of 'strike' applied to striking palms together in ceremony or emphasis. Spanish batieron ('they clapped') and Arabic safaqa ('to clap') mark this as distinct. Joash's coronation (2 Kgs 11:12) and Ezekiel's prophetic gesture (Ezek 21:14) provide the liturgical and rhetorical contexts.
senses.10: At Exod 9:31–32 — the hail 'struck down' the flax and barley but not the wheat. The Pual passive (nukketa) describes crops being beaten down by weather. Spanish fueron golpeados ('were struck') and the agricultural context distinguish this from military or divine-punishment senses.
senses.11: Non-verbal or misassigned tokens: 1 Sam 4:13 (a ketiv-qere marginal note) and 2 Kgs 3:24 (a possible parsing error). English '[ketiv-side]' and Spanish '[junto]' signal these need manual review and likely belong to a different lemma or text-critical category.
senses.12: At Num 22:6 — Balak asks Balaam to come 'that I may strike them' (Israel). Spanish golpear and French a frapper maintain the basic 'strike' meaning, but the context of cursing-as-striking gives it a magical/imprecatory edge unique in the corpus.
senses.13: At Hos 14:5 (ET 14:6) — God 'shall strike' like a flourishing tree sending out roots, or alternately 'strike' in judgment. Spanish echara and French frappa suggest striking in the sense of driving forth or casting out, with prophetic ambiguity between judgment and restoration.
senses.14: At 2 Sam 11:15 — the Niphal 'and he shall be struck and die,' David's instruction to place Uriah in battle's hottest point. Spanish sera herido ('he will be wounded') and the passive construction foreground the victim, making this the sole Niphal occurrence in a calculated-murder context.
senses.15: At 1 Sam 2:14 — the priest's servant 'struck' the fork into the pot. Spanish metia ('inserted/thrust') and the cultic-kitchen context show a non-violent, utilitarian 'thrust/plunge' action, extending nakah's semantics from violent striking to forceful insertion of an implement.

gloss_terse: To attend to, visit, number, appoint, punish; covers census-taking, divine visitation, oversight, and absence
gloss_readable: Few Hebrew verbs span such a wide conceptual arc as paqad. At its root lies the idea of focused attention — but that attention can manifest as counting soldiers for war (Numbers 1), visiting the barren Sarah with a child (Gen 21:1), punishing iniquity to the third generation (Exod 20:5), or appointing an overseer (Gen 39:4). The connecting thread is authoritative notice: someone in charge turns their gaze toward something and acts. Arabic confirms the fragmentation — 'adda for counting, iftaqada for caring visitation, 'aqaba for punishing, and 'ayyana for appointing are four separate roots. The Nifal adds the haunting sense of 'being missed,' as when David's seat at Saul's table sits empty (1 Sam 20:18, 25).

senses.1: The Qal passive participle used substantivally: 'the numbered ones' or 'those enrolled,' appearing 76 times almost exclusively in Numbers' census lists (Num 1:21ff). Arabic al-ma'duduna, Korean gyesu-doen jadeul, and Hindi gine gaye all render 'the counted ones.' This is paqad at its most administrative — headcount as military logistics.
senses.2: To visit with punishment or bring divine judgment — the negative face of God's attention. Exod 20:5 ('visiting the iniquity of the fathers') and Jer 11:22 ('I will punish them') show paqad as retributive divine action. Arabic 'aqaba ('to punish') and Korean beolhada confirm a distinct punitive sense separate from the positive visitation of Sense 4.
senses.3: The active Qal sense of counting, numbering, or mustering — the census-commander's action that produces the passive 'numbered ones' of Sense 1. Extensively used in Numbers (Num 1:3, 1:19, 1:44) and David's census (2 Sam 24). Arabic 'adda/ahsa and Hindi ginna confirm enumeration as the core meaning.
senses.4: To visit someone with gracious attention, care for, or remember — the positive face of divine notice. God 'visited' Sarah and she conceived (Gen 21:1), Joseph prophesied God would 'surely visit' Israel in Egypt (Gen 50:24–25). Arabic iftaqada ('to check on, care for') and Korean dolboda ('to look after') confirm benevolent concern.
senses.5: The Hifil causative: to appoint or set someone in charge over something. Joseph appointed over Potiphar's house (Gen 39:4–5), overseers set over the land (Gen 41:34), Levites appointed over the tabernacle (Num 1:50). Arabic 'ayyana/aqama ('to appoint/install') and Korean immyeonghada confirm institutional authority-delegation.
senses.6: The Nifal: to be missing, lacking, or absent from one's expected place. David's empty seat at the feast (1 Sam 20:18, 25) and the post-battle headcount finding no soldier missing (Num 31:49) illustrate the poignant 'noticed absence' that is paqad's passive counterpart. Arabic yufqad ('to be lost/missing') and Korean ppajida ('to be absent') confirm the gap-detection meaning.
senses.7: The Qal active sense of appointing someone to a position or charging with a task — overlapping with Hifil Sense 5 but in the basic stem. Joseph 'appointed' a guard over the imprisoned butler (Gen 40:4), Israel told to 'appoint' officers (Deut 20:9). Arabic awsa/amara ('to command/charge') adds a commissioning nuance.
senses.8: The Hitpael: to be numbered or enrolled — the reflexive/passive of census-taking. Used when a tribe is exempted from counting (Num 1:47, Levites) or when a total is given (Num 2:33, 26:62). Arabic yu'add ('to be counted') and Korean se'eojida confirm the middle-voice enrollment sense.
senses.9: The Nifal of being visited or punished — the passive of both positive and negative divine attention. Num 16:29 ('if these men are visited with the common fate of all men') tests whether God has truly sent Moses. Arabic yuftaqad and the ambiguity between care and punishment distinguish this passive from the active Senses 2 and 4.
senses.10: The Hofal passive participle: 'the appointed ones' — those who have been placed in positions of oversight. Concentrated in Kings and Chronicles for temple treasurers and construction supervisors (2 Kgs 12:11, 22:5, 2 Chr 34:10). Arabic al-muwakkalina ('those entrusted') and Korean immyeong-doen jadeul confirm institutional title usage.
senses.11: The Hifil sense of depositing or entrusting something to someone's care — a fiduciary meaning. Rehoboam deposited shields with the guard (1 Kgs 14:27, 2 Chr 12:10), and the psalmist commits his spirit into God's hands (Ps 31:5). Arabic awda'a ('to deposit/entrust') maps precisely, marking a transfer-of-custody meaning distinct from appointment.
senses.12: To miss someone's presence, seek, or long for — the emotional dimension of noticing absence. Saul 'misses' David at the feast (1 Sam 20:6), no one 'seeks' the ark (Jer 3:16), and God 'seeks out' every creature (Isa 34:16). Arabic talab/taftaqid ('to seek/miss') and Korean chajda ('to look for') confirm longing-search.
senses.13: The Qal passive participle used as a title: officer or overseer (paqid). Military commanders 'over thousands and hundreds' (Num 31:14, 48) and temple officers (2 Kgs 11:15). Arabic wukala'/quwwad ('agents/commanders') and Korean jihwigwan ('commander') confirm a lexicalized title derived from the 'appointed' participle.
senses.14: At Isa 13:4 — God 'mustering' the armies of judgment. Spanish pasa revista ('reviews troops') and the military-assembly context show active marshaling of forces, combining the census sense (Sense 3) with divine military command in a prophetic-apocalyptic register.
senses.15: At Isa 38:10 — Hezekiah's lament: 'I am deprived of the remainder of my years.' Spanish soy privado ('I am deprived') reinterprets paqad as having something taken away or being cut off from life's expected allotment. A unique existential-loss usage at the boundary between 'being visited' and 'being missing.'
